articles.title: Tension at Nagarjunasagar as A.P. releases water to right canal unilaterally
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Tension prevailed on Nagarjunasagar dam on Thursday afternoon after the irrigation engineers of Andhra Pradesh unilaterally started releasing water to the right canal (NSJC), though no decision was taken on water release at the November 23 three-member committee meeting of the Krishna River Management Board (KRMB), despite the opposition from the Telangana authorities citing lack of approval from the board.

The A.P. engineers did not heed to their Telangana counterparts’ pleas asking not to release water till a decision in the river board meeting, and continued water release. Telangana engineers followed suit and started water release to the left canal (NSLC) an hour later.

Water release from the reservoir unilaterally is set to deplete the water level and storage further and reduce the availability during the critical summer season extending into the next monsoon season, till the arrival of fresh flood. The fresh incident adds to the unease already prevailing between the two States following A.P. taking up a tunnel project from Nagarajunasagar reservoir to draw water for Palnadu water grid with gravity and without approval of the river board and consent of Telangana.

Sources in the Telangana Irrigation department stated that the A.P. irrigation authorities had started drawing water in the guise of meeting drinking water needs. They were planning to increase the drawl to 15,000 cusecs.

As per the joint projects’ management protocol issued by the KRMB, the Nagarajunasagar project is mandated to be operated, including taking care of its maintenance works by the Telangana Irrigation department and that of Srisailam by A.P. Water Resources department. However, A.P. has been repeatedly operating the right canal unilaterally.

According the Nagarjunasagar engineers, water release to the right canal was increased to 6,395 cusecs by A.P. engineers till 6 p.m. and the Telangana engineers gradually increased water release to the left canal to 5,580 cusecs.

articles.title: SCR surpasses rooftop solar target, commissions 6.9 MW capacity
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: South Central Railway (SCR) has commissioned 6.9 MW of rooftop solar power capacity over the past 31 months, surpassing the 4.8 MW target set by the Railway Board under the Prime Minister’s rooftop solar initiative aimed at promoting renewable energy and reducing dependence on conventional power sources.

In a press release issued on Thursday, SCR General Manager Sanjay Kumar Srivastava said the zone has also taken up the installation and commissioning of an additional 2.5 MWp rooftop solar capacity, with work currently in progress.

SCR has utilised rooftop spaces across railway establishments in the Secunderabad, Hyderabad and Nanded divisions, as well as the Lalaguda Workshop, for the installation of solar power plants. These systems generate clean energy at the point of consumption while helping reduce carbon emissions and the overall environmental footprint of railway operations.

Secunderabad Division has commissioned 2.93 MWp of rooftop solar capacity, followed by Hyderabad Division with 2.60 MWp, Lalaguda Workshop with 0.87 MWp, and Nanded Division with 0.50 MWp. Railway officials said the initiative is a significant step towards Indian Railways’ goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2030.

SCR said that during the last three financial years — 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27 — its rooftop solar installations generated 7.32 million units (MU) of electricity. This helped avoid an estimated 4,963 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions, contributing to environmental sustainability and reduced energy costs.

Mr. Srivastava commended the efforts of the railway’s electrical department in implementing the solar projects and said Indian Railways has a major responsibility in developing a greener and more sustainable transportation network.

articles.title: Initiative to take Constitution Day event to taluk centres welcomed
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Constitution is not merely a book or a document but a beacon of hope for the poor, a source of confidence for the oppressed, a symbol of dignity for women and a force that shapes the future of young people, Minister for Backward Classes Welfare and Kannada and Culture and Koppal district in-charge Shivraj Tangadagi has said.

He was speaking after inaugurating the district-level Constitution Day celebrations organised by the district administration, Zilla Panchayat and the Department of Social Welfare at the cultural auditorium of the Kannada and Culture Department in Karatagi on Thursday.

Mr. Tangadagi said that the significance of Constitution Day should reach children and the general public. The values of the Constitution, the principles of democracy and the contributions of B.R. Ambedkar should always be remembered.

“Dr. Ambedkar ensured equal voting rights for every citizen, irrespective of whether they are rich or poor. The Constitution has also provided opportunities for people from ordinary families to become legislators and Ministers,” he said.

Observing that celebrations of important days have traditionally been confined to district headquarters, he welcomed the initiative to extend Constitution Day programmes to taluk centres. He said that the practice should continue and help children, young people and senior citizens understand the importance of the Constitution.
Describing the Constitution as a guiding framework for Ministers, legislators, officials and citizens, he urged everyone to understand its ideals and uphold its values.
He also called upon people to read about the history of the Constitution and remember the efforts and hardships endured by Dr. Ambedkar in drafting it.
Referring to discussions about changing the Constitution, Mr. Tangadagi warned that any attempt to alter its fundamental character will invite strong resistance and serious consequences.
Delivering a special lecture, Gavisiddappa Muttal of Yelburga taluk said that after India gained Independence in 1947, the Constitution was adopted in 1949 and subsequently, it came into force.
It guarantees fundamental rights and creates opportunities for improving people’s lives, he said.

“Equality, liberty, fraternity, educational and political rights and the right to constitutional remedies are among the important safeguards provided by the Constitution. It has also given ordinary citizens equal opportunities to attain political power and serves as the foundation for individual development and a better life,” he said.

However, even 76 years after the Constitution came into force, untouchability and social, political and economic inequalities continue to exist in several places, including rural areas, which is a matter of concern, he added.

articles.title: Jharkhand Government lauds CSIR-NML’s contribution to India’s industrial development
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Jharkhand Governor Santosh Kumar Gangwar on Thursday (November 26, 2026) lauded the CSIR-National Metallurgical Laboratory (NML) for establishing a distinct identity in the fields of minerals, metals and materials science, and making significant contributions to the country’s industrial development.

Addressing the 77th Foundation Day celebrations of CSIR-NML in the steel city, Mr. Gangwar expressed pleasure at being part of the occasion and congratulated the institute’s scientists, researchers, technical officers, employees and their family members.

He said the true identity of an institution was established through its contribution to the nation and society over the years, adding that the institute’s journey spanning more than seven decades was a matter of pride and inspiration.

“The identity of the industrial city of Jamshedpur is closely associated with industry, hard work and technological development. The Tata Group, along with the workers, engineers and entrepreneurs of this region, has played a significant role in making it a major centre of industrial progress,” he said.
A rich tradition of education and research had also evolved in the region, and the presence of a prestigious institution like CSIR-NML held special significance, he added.
Over the past 76 years, the institute has established a distinct identity in the fields of minerals, metals and materials science, the governor said.

Through research, experiments and the development of new technologies, scientists and researchers at the laboratory have made significant contributions to the country’s industrial development, he said.

Important work was being undertaken at the institute in areas such as extracting useful materials from minerals, developing strong and durable metals and materials, and recycling and reusing industrial waste, Mr. Gangwar added.
He also highlighted the growing demand for critical minerals and speciality metals for national development, modern industries and the defence sector.

“Natural resources are invaluable assets of our country, and by ensuring their optimum utilisation through scientific research, we can give new impetus to our economic and industrial progress,” he said.

Mr. Gangwar also highlighted the growing use of semiconductors and advanced materials in mobile phones, computers, defence equipment and modern machinery, emphasising the need to develop indigenous technologies.

Under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and guided by the mantra ‘Jai Vigyan, Jai Anusandhan’, innovation and research in the country were receiving fresh direction and momentum, he said.

articles.title: Karnataka CM D.K. Shivakumar tells striking ASHA workers not to ‘blackmail’ government
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: As ASHA workers continued their indefinite day-and-night protest at Freedom Park in Bengaluru for the 10th consecutive day, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar on Thursday told the striking workers not to “blackmail” the government and urged them to resume duty, assuring that the government would look into their demands.

Speaking to reporters at Mysuru airport, Mr. Shivakumar said he had spoken to the ASHA workers over phone during his Japan tour and appealed to them to withdraw their strike. He urged them to have faith in the government and its assurance against their demands.

Expressing dissatisfaction over the workers’ decision to continue their agitation, he said, “They cannot blackmail the government. I once again appeal to them to end their strike and return to their duties.”
The Chief Minister rejected the demand for a written assurance, saying that accepting such a condition would encourage similar demands from other organisations.

“If I give this in writing, everyone will come up with similar demands. There are demands from 17 such organisations. The government has its limitations. I cannot give anything in writing, but they must have faith in the government and in the word of the Chief Minister. Otherwise, I cannot do anything,” he said.

“There cannot be an agreement when it comes to meeting demands. However, as I have assured them, I will look into the matter. I am not saying their demands are unjustified. Everyone will make demands, but they must have faith,” he said. He added that a decision on their demands would be taken at the Cabinet and during the Legislature session.

Meanwhile, speaking in Bengaluru, Health Minister U.T. Khader too expressed displeasure over the continued protest, questioning why the government should trust them if they were unwilling to repose faith in its assurances. He also claimed that healthcare services had continued without major disruption despite the workers staying away from duty for 10 days.

Mr. Khader said the government had sought time to examine their demands and promised to arrive at a decision by the end of the upcoming legislature session after consultations with the Finance Department, legislators and the Cabinet.
“If they do not have faith in us and do not trust what we have said, then why should we have faith in them?” he asked, expressing disappointment over their refusal to call off the agitation.

The Minister pointed out that the State government was already providing an additional ₹5,000 to ASHA workers over and above the Centre’s contribution. Their demand for a monthly honorarium of ₹15,000 needed careful consideration as it involved around 41,000 workers and had wider financial implications, he said.

articles.title: Congress leader Manickam Tagore questions Udhayanidhi’s meeting with Tamil Nadu Governor
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Tamil Nadu Congress Committee (TNCC) president and Virudhunagar MP B. Manickam Tagore on Thursday (November 26, 2026) questioned Leader of Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin’s decision to meet Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar and submit a petition, recalling his earlier remarks describing the Governor as a “postman.”
Mr. Tagore asked how the DMK leader could now approach the same constitutional authority after having questioned his authority and made disparaging remarks about his office.

Addressing mediapersons along with Higher Education Minister P. Viswanathan and Tourism Minister S. Rajesh Kumar at Chennai, he also raised questions about whether there had been an “understanding” between the DMK and the BJP on the delimitation issue and whether the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) cases against DMK leaders had been settled. “Udhayanidhi and the DMK must first answer these questions,” he said.

Responding to a question on the Congress’s own position on the Governor, given that its Ministers had approached him on matters concerning the appointment of Vice-Chancellors, Mr. Tagore said the Congress had never opposed the institution of the Governor.

“The Congress believes that the Governor’s post should continue and that the person holding the office must act impartially and remain above politics. The Governor should provide accurate information to the Union government, work in coordination with the State government and not create unnecessary friction between the two,” he said.

On the allegations concerning the Kallakurichi MLA and the complaint lodged by a woman IAS officer , Mr. Tagore said a fair investigation should be allowed to proceed and those found guilty should face action. He maintained that the safety of women, particularly those working in public institutions, was paramount.

“If anyone has committed a mistake, it is the government’s duty to conduct a proper investigation and punish them. Women have struggled for generations to enter education and the workforce. Ensuring their safety is everyone’s responsibility. Those holding positions of responsibility must be doubly careful,” he said.

“This is not merely the TVK government. This is the government of the secular social justice alliance , comprising the TVK, Congress, VCK and IUML. We are equally responsible for its successes and failures. We will support the government where necessary and point out its shortcomings wherever required,” he said.

articles.title: Experts say new U.S. tariffs do not pose substantial threat, India should not rush into trade deal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The new 25% tariffs proposed by the U.S. on India do not pose a substantial risk to Indian exports, and India should go ahead with a trade deal only if it is balanced and reciprocal, according to exporters and trade and tariff experts.

An analysis of India’s trade relationship with the U.S. over the last two years showed that the latest tariffs announced by the U.S. have returned the tariff relationship to where it was at the start of trade deal negotiations.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed a net tariff of 25% on goods imported from India, which could be reduced to 17% if a trade deal is signed by the two countries.

The tariffs are not final yet, with the U.S. government opening a window for written comments and requests to testify by January 5, 2027. Public hearings will begin on January 25, 2027, following which the final action will be communicated.

The proposed 25% tariff is nearly the same as the 26% tariff U.S. President Donald Trump had originally proposed in his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariff measure in April 2025. A week later, Mr. Trump paused these tariffs in a bid to secure trade deals with other countries.

In July 2025, he announced a 25% tariff on India, the same as what the USTR is now proposing. But Mr. Trump soon announced an additional 25% tariff as a penalty for India’s Russian oil imports taking the total tariff on Indian goods to 50%.

During that time, Mr. Trump also announced a 50% tariff on the import of steel and aluminium from all countries. The latest tariffs by the USTR are not in addition to those tariffs, meaning Indian steel and aluminium will continue to attract a 50% duty.

In February 2026, India and the U.S. issued a joint statement announcing the framework for an interim deal on trade, under which the U.S. would reduce its tariffs on Indian goods to 18%. This is very close to the 17% the U.S. is proposing now, should a deal be signed, nearly 10 months after the joint statement was issued.
As such, the pre-deal, post-deal, and steel and aluminium tariffs by the U.S. on India largely remain where they were at the start of negotiations.
Exporters and trade experts have said that India should proceed with a trade deal only if it satisfies Indian interests.

“FIEO supports the government’s efforts to conclude the Bilateral Trade Agreement at an early date,” said S.C. Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. “The agreement should be balanced and reciprocal, safeguard India’s long-term economic and developmental interests, and ensure that Indian exporters can compete on a level-playing field with suppliers from other countries in the U.S. market.”

The president of the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Anil Gupta, pointed out that the tariffs will have a limited impact on Indian exports due to the nature of the commodities that India predominantly exports to the U.S.

articles.title: Broad-based pressure on food prices continues: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: High-frequency data up to November 19 indicate continuing broad-based pressure on food prices, according to the November edition of the RBI Bulletin, released on Wednesday. .
Prices of all major cereals and pulses picked up. Edible oil prices recorded a broad-based increase, led by mustard oil, the RBI officials said in the State of the Economy article.

Vegetable prices presented a mixed picture, with onion prices rising moderately, tomato prices correcting sharply and potato prices picking up. The Indian basket of crude oil declined to $95 per barrel during November 1-18.
“The pressure on prices was primarily driven by ‘food and beverages’,” the officials pointed out.
Inflationary pressures were, however, not confined to food. Fuel and core inflation also firmed up, with 11 of the 12 CPI divisions registering sequential increases in October.

Within food and beverages, inflation rose across most sub-components, with notable spikes in vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats, reflecting positive month-on-month price momentum. Fuel inflation recorded a relatively moderate uptick.

Geographically, inflation increased in both rural and urban areas in October, with food and beverages inflation remaining above 6% in both segments. While most States and Union Territories recorded inflation in the 4-6% range, the number reporting rates above 6% increased.

On the external front, geopolitical instability in West Asia continued to weigh on the global economic outlook. Although crude oil prices retreated from their October peaks, the absence of a durable peace kept markets volatile. “Apart from extant geopolitical risks, the recent pullback in AI stocks lends uncertainty to the global financial outlook,” the officials said.

Despite the challenging global environment and hawkish monetary policy stances adopted by major central banks, the RBI maintained that India’s domestic growth drivers and macroeconomic fundamentals remained important buffers.
“The Indian economy continues to maintain the resilience in economic activities as evident from high-frequency indicators,” they said.
“Strong bank and non-bank credit growth continues to support the domestic economy. Further, sustained double-digit export growth broadened the base of economic expansion,” they added.
Equity markets remained buoyant amid robust corporate earnings and foreign portfolio investment inflows, while net inflows through external commercial borrowings and NRI deposits remained strong.

articles.title: Net FDI fell to more than 5.5-year low in September 2026, as outflows jumped 40%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India in September 2026 fell to its lowest level in at least 5.5 years, with outflows exceeding inflows by nearly $5 billion, data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shows.

This was driven by a simultaneous slump in gross inflows and a jump in outflows. However, net FDI in the first half of the financial year (April-September 2026) was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
September’s net FDI figure of -$4.95 billion was the lowest since at least March 2021, the earliest month for which data is accessible.

Direct investment refers to the inflows that give the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production, as opposed to portfolio investments, which are typically more in the nature of speculative purchases of minor shareholding.
Gross inflows, or the total amount of direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September 2026, 46.6% lower than in August, and 17.6% lower than in September of last year.

According to the RBI, around two-thirds of the gross inflows were channelled into manufacturing, communication, and computer services sectors, with Singapore and the U.S. as the major source countries.

Total outflows climbed to $10.8 billion in September 2026, nearly 40% higher than in August, and 15% higher than in September last year. Within this, repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India grew to $6.4 billion, nearly 37% higher than in the same month last year, and the highest since at least March 2021.
Outward investments made by Indian companies grew to a five-month high of $4.4 billion in September 2026.

The RBI says that of the outward investments, manufacturing, and financial, insurance and business services sectors accounted for about four-fifths of the amount that flowed out of India, with The Netherlands, Singapore and the U.S. serving as the major destinations.

articles.title: Duty-free raw sugar imports up to 10 lakh tonnes allowed till March 2027
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar will be permitted until the end of March 2027, according to a notification issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) on Wednesday.

A notification issued on August 20 had allowed duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of sugar under the Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) scheme until December 31, 2026. Separately, the DGFT has allowed sugar mills time until September 30, 2027, to process the imported raw sugar and sell it in the domestic market.

The Indian Sugar and Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association Director General Deepak Ballani told The Hindu that price parity had prevailed over the past, making it viable for Indian importers to source raw sugar from international markets, primarily Brazil. Some imports have already begun.

The industry expects more imports in the coming days and this will ensure supply of adequate quantity of sugar in the domestic market throughout the sugar season. It will also keep the prices stable, he said.

articles.title: Air passenger services see 35% inflation in Q2; banking, securities transaction witness deflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Air passenger services recorded 35.52% inflation in the July-September quarter, recording the highest rate of price rise among the seven major services for which the inflation data was released on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Securities transaction services and banking services, however, recorded a deflation of 6.93% and 3.96% respectively, the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27 released by the Commerce and Industry Ministry showed.
The PPI has inflation data for seven major services — Banking, Securities Transaction, Insurance, Management of Pension Funds, Railways, Air (Passenger), and Telecom — with base year 2022-23.
Service PPI measures the change in the average prices received by producers on production of a service.
As per the data, inflation in Air (Passenger) Services rose 35.52% YoY in the second quarter, compared to 31.94% in the first quarter.
Annual inflation in the railway passenger service price index rose 2.17% during the September quarter, lower than 3.50% in the June quarter.
Inflation in 'Banking Service Contribution' was 3.86% in Q2 of FY27, higher than 2.62% in Q1. The 'Banking Service Price' witnessed 3.96% deflation in Q2, vis-a-vis 4.98% deflation in Q1.
Securities Transaction Service Prices saw a deflation of 6.93% in Q2, compared to 1.32% deflation in June quarter.

Pension fund management, insurance and telecom services recorded an inflation of 1.01%, 0.49% and 0.54%, respectively in September quarter, compared to 5.48%, 0.98% and 0.72%, respectively in the June quarter.
The government would eventually include more services in the Service PPI data.

The government in June came out with the maiden PPI data for both goods and services to better reflect price movement at producer's level, paving the way for phasing out wholesale price index (WPI)-based inflation numbers in the next five years. Thereafter, in August the services PPI data was issued.

articles.title: Global climate talks must shut door on fossil fuel ‘clout’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The failure of the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, to agree on its central political statement, with countries unable to bridge their differences over fossil fuels and other key questions of climate action, has exposed the fragility of international climate cooperation. It should also sharpen scrutiny of who gets access to climate negotiations, whose interests they represent and what safeguards keep decisions accountable to the public.

The Türkiye summit ended without agreement on an overarching statement. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he shared the “deep disappointment” of many that the conference was unable to reach consensus on a statement that typically sends a policy signal to all nations. Some separate negotiating decisions were reached though. Nevertheless, the absence of a political consensus was a serious setback.

The breakdown does not show that fossil fuel lobbying caused the impasse. But it does make more urgent a separate question about the credibility of the process. A forum that asks governments to make decisions in the global public interest must be transparent about who is seeking to shape those decisions, what interests they represent and how conflicts are managed.

The international climate negotiations that take place every year still lack a comprehensive, enforceable system to identify and manage conflicts of interest involving powerful commercial interests, including fossil fuel companies and state-owned energy businesses. The Antalya conference has underlined why that gap matters.

The fossil fuel industry’s record of muddying the waters is well documented. A 2017 study by Geoffrey Supran and Naomi Oreskes compared 187 ExxonMobil communications between 1977 and 2014, including internal documents, scientific publications and paid newspaper advertorials. It found that as the company’s communications became more public, they increasingly expressed doubt about climate science. The researchers concluded that ExxonMobil had contributed to climate science while promoting doubt about it in its advertorials.

An industry team discussed a 1998 draft of the Global Climate Science Communications Plan at the American Petroleum Institute’s headquarters. The plan’s stated goal was to persuade a majority of the American public that significant uncertainties remained in climate science and to raise questions among policymakers.

This history matters because companies with large investments in oil, gas and coal have a financial stake in how quickly those fuels are phased down, which technologies receive support and how the costs of the transition are distributed. That does not mean every company representative at a climate summit is there to obstruct progress, or that attendance proves influence over a decision. It, however, does mean commercial interests need to be visible and the process needs rules to prevent undue influence.

The scale of corporate participation in Antalya brings the issue into sharper focus. An analysis by a coalition of non-profits identified 103 major polluter groups with delegations at the summit, including fossil fuel businesses, financiers and companies from other high-emitting sectors. It also identified 30 banks whose fossil fuel financing between 2021 and 2025 amounted to more than $2.2 trillion.

These are the coalition’s classifications, not official UN figures. They do not establish that the companies or banks influenced the negotiations. But they show the scale of commercial interests present at a conference whose purpose is to limit global warming.

Lien Vandamme of the Center for International Environmental Law says the problem goes beyond the number of corporate participants. Although the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has introduced limited disclosure requirements, she argues that it still lacks a policy to curb corporate influence. “There is currently no policy to curb corporate influence within the UNFCCC process, and this is a fundamental problem,” she says. Once companies gain access, she argues, it becomes extremely difficult to monitor how they use it to influence negotiations.

The distinction between access and proven influence matters. The presence of a company representative does not show that a final decision was shaped by that company. But without public information about who participants represent, who funds their participation and what interests they promote and advance, it is difficult to assess where influence may be exercised.

The issue also extends beyond private companies. Some governments are major producers of oil and gas, while state-owned energy firms have direct commercial interests in the outcome of climate negotiations. Safeguards that examine only private corporations would leave a substantial part of the problem untouched.

articles.title: Serbia sets Presidential election for December 27 after students won Parliamentary vote
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Serbia 's Parliament speaker on Thursday (November 26, 2026) set an early Presidential election for December 27, after former President Aleksandar Vucic resigned in September to pursue what turned out to be a failed bid to become Prime Minister.
The Presidential vote will be held after a student movement defeated Mr. Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party in an early Parliamentary ballot on October 25.

Mr. Vucic and his party had ruled virtually unchallenged for 14 years. He had run for Prime Minister after serving two near-complete five-year terms as President, and was banned by law from seeking a third term.
“I hope we will have a tough choice between top candidates and their programmes," Speaker Aleksandar Cupic said. “Building democratic institutions is the task for all of us.”
It was not immediately clear who the Presidential candidates will be. Mr. Vucic has suggested that his SNS party could sit out the election.

The Presidency in Serbia is largely ceremonial. The President commands the Army and has a say in foreign policy but has no executive powers. While he was in office, however, Mr. Vucic concentrated power in the Presidency, facing accusations of authoritarian rule. Mr. Vucic regularly announced important state decisions and policies and even presided over government sessions.

Since losing power, Mr. Vucic has accused the election winners of imposing a “revolutionary terror,” although his government is still technically in control until a new one is formed. The change in power has led to a surge in detentions of officials and police officers suspected of abusing their positions during Mr. Vucic's rule.

The youth-led movement had led two years of street protests that started in response to a train station canopy collapse in northern Serbia that killed 16 people. Many blamed the tragedy on alleged rampant corruption and negligence during the building renovation in Novi Sad.

articles.title: U.K. net migration falls to lowest since 1997; Indians largest foreign group entering and leaving the country
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Net migration to the U.K. has fallen to 77,000, its lowest levels since 1997, excluding the pandemic, as per official U.K. government figures released on Thursday (November 26, 2026). Indians constituted the largest foreign nationality group immigrating and emigrating longterm to and from the U.K.

The net migration figure, which represents the number of people arriving in the U.K. minus those emigrating, fell dramatically from 2,04,000 for the year ending June 2025 and from a record high of 9,00,000 in the year ending June 2023. The news is likely to a shot in the arm for the governing Labour Party, as migration has become a political lighting-rod in recent years.

The latest drop in numbers was predominantly due to a fall in non-EU migration to the U.K. This figure fell by more then 1,00,000 while emigration remained mostly stable. Non-EU+ nationals arriving in the U.K. fell by 17% to 7,38,000. Just under half came to study, a quarter for work, and 13% for asylum.

Of those migrating to the U.K., the largest group consisted of Indians , then Chinese, then Nigerians, Pakistanis and Americans. Some 44,000 Indians arrived in the U.K. for work-related reasons, 77,000 to study, and 5,000 for other reasons. Some 28,000 Indians on work visas left the U.K. and 55,000 on study visas departed.
More EU+ and British nationals left the U.K. than non-EU+ nationals. Some 2,45,00 Britons left the country longterm in the year ending June 2026, with net migration of Britons at -1,37,000.

These record high net migration numbers in 2023 — called the ‘Boriswave’, occurred during the administration of Boris Johnson, a Conservative, following Brexit and the COVID-19 pandemic, when visa rules were eased to fill certain occupations such as social care. Migration from non-EU countries consequently increased at this time. Mr. Johnson’s successors, Rishi Sunak, a fellow Conservative, and then Prime Minister Keir Starmer of the Labour Party, further tightened immigration policies resulting in falling numbers.

fullParagraphs: German prosecutors said on Thursday (November 26, 2026) they had arrested two Iraqi nationals suspected ​of belonging to a terrorist organisation that plotted attacks ‌on Jewish and other targets in Europe, including ​a Cologne synagogue.

Germany has suffered a series ⁠of attacks and plots in recent years, including a fatal attack in July in which a man who pledged ‌allegiance to Islamic State attacked a Pride celebration in Berlin. Jewish institutions are under heightened protection after warnings of threats linked ‌to ⁠West Asia tensions.

Prosecutors said officers had ⁠detained Mostafa Al-R. in Heidelberg and Ameer J. in Cologne, with their full names withheld in line with privacy rules, following ​17 raids in ‌the states of Baden-Wuerttemberg, Hesse and North Rhine-Westphalia.

They said Mostafa Al-R. had ties to Mohammad Al-Saadi, an alleged member of an Islamist group that ‌has said it was behind a series ​of attacks on U.S., Israeli and Jewish facilities in Europe since March.

Prosecutors said that ⁠Al-Saadi, Mostafa Al-R. and others had formed a separate organisation in late 2025 to prepare further attacks ‌in Germany and elsewhere in Europe. Ameer J. was a member of that group, they said.
It recruited external operatives and raised funds for explosives attacks, prosecutors said.

They said that on two consecutive nights in late March, unidentified individuals suspected of ‌acting on the group's behalf and carrying explosive devices ​had travelled to a synagogue in Cologne and another unspecified location in Europe, but no ⁠attacks were carried out for reasons that were ⁠unclear.
The two suspects were due on Thursday (November 26, 2026) to appear before a Judge who will ‌decide whether they remain in pre-trial detention.
Authorities said the investigation was launched because of intelligence supplied ​by Germany's domestic intelligence agency.

articles.title: Situation in India-China border areas remains ‘generally stable’, says China
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The situation in the India-China border areas remain “generally stable”, China’s Defence Ministry spokesperson and PLA Senior Colonel Chen Xi said on Thursday (November 26, 2026) adding that China “does not recognize the so-called Arunachal Pradesh illegally set up by India.”

“China and India maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels, including general-level talks, to jointly implement the consensus reached by the two sides and safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas”, he said in response to a question at a press briefing on recent tensions in the Eastern sector of the border, Chinese state media reported.

On November 24, 2026, India and China concluded a second round of Corps Commander-level talks aimed at easing tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh and putting in place measures to prevent friction between troops deployed along the frontier ahead of the onset of harsh winter conditions.

Sources in the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the closely guarded discussions, which began on November 8, 2026, a day after Deepavali, continued for nearly 10 days, with a short break in between. The talks were described as cordial, though it remains unclear whether the measures discussed will be implemented on the ground before winter sets in fully.

The latest round of talks primarily focused on establishing engagement protocols between the two sides, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops deployed along the frontier, maintaining open communication channels and reducing tensions in the eastern sector. Both countries have deployed substantial numbers of troops in the region.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The new 25% tariffs proposed by the U.S. on India do not pose a substantial risk to Indian exports, and India should go ahead with a trade deal only if it is balanced and reciprocal, according to exporters and trade and tariff experts.

An analysis of India’s trade relationship with the U.S. over the last two years showed that the latest tariffs announced by the U.S. have returned the tariff relationship to where it was at the start of trade deal negotiations.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed a net tariff of 25% on goods imported from India, which could be reduced to 17% if a trade deal is signed by the two countries.

The tariffs are not final yet, with the U.S. government opening a window for written comments and requests to testify by January 5, 2027. Public hearings will begin on January 25, 2027, following which the final action will be communicated.

The proposed 25% tariff is nearly the same as the 26% tariff U.S. President Donald Trump had originally proposed in his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariff measure in April 2025. A week later, Mr. Trump paused these tariffs in a bid to secure trade deals with other countries.

In July 2025, he announced a 25% tariff on India, the same as what the USTR is now proposing. But Mr. Trump soon announced an additional 25% tariff as a penalty for India’s Russian oil imports taking the total tariff on Indian goods to 50%.

During that time, Mr. Trump also announced a 50% tariff on the import of steel and aluminium from all countries. The latest tariffs by the USTR are not in addition to those tariffs, meaning Indian steel and aluminium will continue to attract a 50% duty.

In February 2026, India and the U.S. issued a joint statement announcing the framework for an interim deal on trade, under which the U.S. would reduce its tariffs on Indian goods to 18%. This is very close to the 17% the U.S. is proposing now, should a deal be signed, nearly 10 months after the joint statement was issued.
As such, the pre-deal, post-deal, and steel and aluminium tariffs by the U.S. on India largely remain where they were at the start of negotiations.
Exporters and trade experts have said that India should proceed with a trade deal only if it satisfies Indian interests.

“FIEO supports the government’s efforts to conclude the Bilateral Trade Agreement at an early date,” said S.C. Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. “The agreement should be balanced and reciprocal, safeguard India’s long-term economic and developmental interests, and ensure that Indian exporters can compete on a level-playing field with suppliers from other countries in the U.S. market.”

The president of the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Anil Gupta, pointed out that the tariffs will have a limited impact on Indian exports due to the nature of the commodities that India predominantly exports to the U.S.

articles.title: Indian pharma company Hetero begins supply of generic twice-yearly HIV prevention injection in Africa
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Hyderabad-based pharmaceutical company Hetero has begun phased shipments of generic injectable lenacapavir, a long-acting drug for HIV prevention, to three African countries. The company plans to supply 300,000 vials initially to Zambia, Uganda and Zimbabwe.
Lenacapavir is used as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to reduce the risk of acquiring HIV. Unlike daily oral PrEP medicines, the injectable formulation is administered once every six months.

Hetero is launching the generic drug under the brand names Lexapir and Capvic. The company expects to introduce its generic oral initiation tablets by January 2027. These tablets form part of the PrEP regimen and will be supplied by the original manufacturer, Gilead Sciences, in the interim.

The launch follows Gilead’s non-exclusive voluntary licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers, allowing them to manufacture and supply generic lenacapavir in 120 eligible countries. The licensing arrangement is intended to expand access to the drug in low- and middle-income countries.

Hetero said its generic injectable formulation and oral initiation tablets had received an Expert Review Panel recommendation, allowing eligible procurement through applicable Global Fund channels while regulatory approval or WHO prequalification processes continue. In Zimbabwe, procurement is being supported through the United Nations Development Programme using Global Fund financing.

The company plans to supply the drug to 10 additional African countries in early 2027 and expand availability across other countries covered by its licence, subject to national regulatory approvals and procurement arrangements. It also plans to introduce generic lenacapavir in India in the coming months, subject to regulatory clearance.

articles.title: BITS Pilani-Hyderabad researchers develop affordable way to grow microalgae
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Researchers at BITS Pilani, Hyderabad Campus, have secured an Indian patent for a low-cost nutrient medium that could make large-scale cultivation of microalgae more affordable, opening possibilities for applications in renewable fuels, carbon capture and biotechnology.

The patented innovation, titled “Nutrient Medium Composition for Mass Cultivation of Microalgae” (Patent No. 603126), has been developed by Sandip S. Deshmukh of the Department of Mechanical Engineering, K. Pranav Narayan of the Department of Biological Sciences and research scholar Sama Sanghamitra, as per a press release issued on Thursday (November 26, 2026).

Microalgae are microscopic organisms that use sunlight and carbon dioxide to produce biomass. They are considered a promising resource for wastewater treatment, carbon dioxide capture, biofertilisers, food and nutraceutical products, and the production of biodiesel and other bio-based fuels. However, the high cost of cultivation has limited their large-scale adoption.

The BITS team developed an alternative nutrient formulation using locally available agricultural-grade fertilisers instead of expensive laboratory-grade chemicals. The formulation supplies key nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and sulphur required for microalgal growth while reducing the complexity and cost of preparing the cultivation medium.

The macronutrients needed to prepare 100 litres of the new medium cost about ₹2.40, compared with around ₹43 for the conventional Bold’s Basal Medium (BBM). The cost is estimated to be around ₹4.50 per 100 litres, making it significantly cheaper than conventional alternatives.

The formulation is also easy to prepare and can be supplied as a dry powder, which can be dissolved in water before use. The technology was tested in laboratory, non-sterile and outdoor cultivation conditions. The microalgae was also successfully cultivated in a 10,000-litre open pond using natural sunlight and atmospheric carbon dioxide.

Researchers are now in discussions with a potential industry partner, which has proposed a two-month evaluation of the formulation for carbon capture and biomass production applications. They are also seeking collaborations with companies in biofuel, algal biotechnology and carbon management sectors to explore commercialisation of the technology.

articles.title: IREF say non-basmati rice export bans are unlikely, but urges exporters to remain cautious
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The government is unlikely to impose restrictions on non-basmati rice exports over the next month, the Indian Rice Exporters’ Federation (IREF) said on its portal on Wednesday (November 26, 2026).
It, however, urged rice exporters to continue business with appropriate contractual and inventory safeguards.

The Federation claimed that based on information received from sources familiar with policy discussions, its current assessment was that while policy options remain under consideration, there is no indication of an immediate move to curb exports.
However, the possibility of export duties or other policy measures cannot be ruled out, particularly if domestic rice prices continue to rise.

India’s substantial rice stocks provide an important cushion for domestic supply. The Public Distribution System (PDS), through which eligible households receive subsidised or free foodgrains under their entitlements, also helps protect beneficiaries from fluctuations in open-market prices.
However, strong international demand continues to influence domestic market dynamics. Any further significant icrease in domestic prices can prompt a review of the export policy.

articles.title: Mercury in cosmetics: What does the Kerala case reveal about the health risks of skin-lightening creams? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The quest for beauty and the enduring appeal for fair and blemishfree skin goes back to ages and across cultures. However, in recent years, this has been landing people in hospitals with serious health issues, as it happened in the case of the 17-year-old girl from Areekode in Malappuram district in Kerala.

Persuaded by many social influencers who raved about a face cream which gave them fair, blemishfree skin, she had also been using the same for over a year. The product with the brand name F-TUNES - claimed to contain turmeric and other “natural ingredients” and cited Dubai as the place of manufacture. She was hospitalised after she developed severe symptoms like fainting spells, swelling on legs and fall in blood pressure and was diagnosed with Membranous nephropathy, a condition wherein the immune system gets dysregulated, triggering nephrotic syndrome (heavy loss of protein through urine). Doctors traced her condition to the heavy mercury content in the face cream she was using. Lab analysis of a sample of the skin lightning cream obtained from the patient revealed that the product contained 12,500 ppm of mercury, way over the legal limit of 1 ppm

After prolonged treatment, the girl is now recovering. The police and drug regulatory authorities have begun a crackdown on the dubious cosmetic products in the market . The Health Minister has also threatened action against social influencers who are peddling dubious cosmetics online

articles.title: All to play for: On the World chess championship in Geneva
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The World chess championship opened in Geneva with a game worthy of the occasion. Both the defending champion, D. Gukesh, and his challenger, Javokhir Sindarov, produced chess of top quality, and the draw was a just result . Given that the Indian was playing with black pieces and that he had gone into the match as the less favoured of the two, Gukesh could be a little happier with the game than his Uzbek rival. The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.

Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.
• Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.title: Beyond generosity: on India-Nepal ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The state visit of Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah to Delhi, eight months after he was voted to power as leader of the ‘GenZ’ movement that ousted the previous government, was anticipated as a chance to reset the turbulent India-Nepal relationship. Bringing Mr. Shah to India for a state visit, his first, was particularly important, given the Modi government’s tense ties with his predecessor K.P. Sharma Oli’s government; Mr. Oli was not invited to Delhi more than a year into his term and travelled to Beijing instead. Initially, Mr. Shah had also given New Delhi some worrying moments, with comments about boundary disputes, and a refusal to confirm a meeting with Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, which led to the cancellation of his visit in May. Subsequently, some of the realities of governance, particularly after the massive flash flood in August , have warmed Delhi-Kathmandu relations. Following talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Mr. Shah thanked India for its immediate and unstinting support in the flood relief and rescue operations. Mr. Modi’s praise for Mr. Shah indicated the forging of a personal rapport on which to build the road map for ties. India announced a Development Cooperation Package — a generous ₹15,000 crore (about $1.6 billion) — for reconstruction and long-term development in Nepal. Another announcement, to offer Nepal access to Indian ports in Gujarat and Odisha, will go a long way in helping land-locked Nepal, particularly given the bilateral bad blood over the 2015 trade blockade. The inauguration of bridges, roads, trains, energy and fuel lines, an Integrated Check post (ICP) and an agreement to set up an IIT (its third offshore campus) are all signs of concrete plans to improve relations, as outlined in the joint statement titled “Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal: Re-imagining the Partnership”.

Despite some of the heated rhetoric over ties, both sides appeared to have decided to deal with areas of differences in a less public manner. Mr. Shah’s persistent comments on the boundary dispute, and long-pending request for overflight access for two debt-ridden airports, were not dealt with directly, but in a broad reference about resolving “all outstanding matters” through dialogue. While the joint statement also said they would review all bilateral treaties, New Delhi’s contention that the “Eminent Persons Group” (EPG) report that suggested important changes to the 1950 Friendship treaty, is now “not relevant”, will ruffle feathers in Kathmandu which has been keen to update the treaty. The government must remember that along with the grand gestures, it is important to keep a close eye on Nepal’s grievances as well. If disregarded, these can trip up the broader progress and conception of the bilateral relationship, as spelt out by both leaders.

articles.title: Spinning wheels: on urban mobility in Karnataka
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: While Karnataka has spent years disputing motorcycle owners’ right to carry paying passengers, Bengaluru — with the dubious distinction of having one of the world’s highest travel times per unit distance — struggles with inadequate public transport capacity and lacklustre intermediate options. The Supreme Court ruling on November 20 to dismiss Karnataka’s appeal was thus straightforward, allowing motorcycles to be registered as transport vehicles. The State has often called bike taxis unsafe, yet has not improved the prospects of safer options. Earlier this year, the Centre for Science and Environment estimated the number of buses in urban centres nationwide to be 70% short of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs benchmark and that 400 cities with populations between a lakh and 10 lakh altogether lacked organised bus services. In March, the BMTC reported a fleet of around 7,000 buses in Bengaluru, versus the 13,000 by 2025 envisaged by the Comprehensive Mobility Plan. Expanding the number of Metro stations also creates more demand for travel to and from stations, but the operating costs of the public transport corporation expected to serve that demand are not covered by the resulting increase in rail ridership.

Overall, Karnataka has struggled to set up a consistent transport policy. An expert committee recommended against bike taxis in Bengaluru for first- and last-mile connectivity and in favour of better walking infrastructure and bicycle rentals in 2019, only for the State to launch the electric bike-taxi scheme in 2021, then rescind it in 2024 over safety concerns and drivers’ disputes. The market for short booked journeys is also dysfunctional. But while allowing bike taxis could temper autorickshaw fares, the State must investigate drivers’ operating costs, the difference between the paid and the received amounts, and prevent large platforms from exploiting the market. Finally, while the Union Road Transport Ministry has reported that 46.2% of all road deaths involved two-wheeler users, two-wheelers’ safety relative to autorickshaws and cabs, by the number and distance of journeys, is unclear. The State should require aggregators to report injuries and fatalities and investigate the consequences of drivers’ earnings being linked to the number of trips undertaken. The Union government’s 2025 Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines already address passenger security, fares, and insurance while allowing States to authorise privately registered motorcycles through aggregators. Karnataka should exercise this additional power. A large national programme is required to address funding for public transport, which is necessary even when it is not immediately profitable.

articles.title: Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement , called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations ; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance.

The increase in solar panel installations and the significant shift towards battery use in grid storage and transport did not come cheap: the cost of the land required for their installation, their intermittent nature of being dependent on weather, grid upgrades all carry costs. It is global markets, imperfectly connected, but connected, that have managed to bring it to this stage over decades. India and China, major fossil emitters, with large, still indigent populations, are also leaders in total clean energy installations. Therefore it stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming. Economic crises are a feature, and not a bug, of the interconnected financial system enveloping the world and there are, undeniably, challenges to diverting the necessary finance towards countries most vulnerable to climate change impact. However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

articles.title: Just verdict: on Myanmar and the International Court of Justice
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy.

The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

articles.title: Tension at Nagarjunasagar as A.P. releases water to right canal unilaterally
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Tension prevailed on Nagarjunasagar dam on Thursday afternoon after the irrigation engineers of Andhra Pradesh unilaterally started releasing water to the right canal (NSJC), though no decision was taken on water release at the November 23 three-member committee meeting of the Krishna River Management Board (KRMB), despite the opposition from the Telangana authorities citing lack of approval from the board.

The A.P. engineers did not heed to their Telangana counterparts’ pleas asking not to release water till a decision in the river board meeting, and continued water release. Telangana engineers followed suit and started water release to the left canal (NSLC) an hour later.

Water release from the reservoir unilaterally is set to deplete the water level and storage further and reduce the availability during the critical summer season extending into the next monsoon season, till the arrival of fresh flood. The fresh incident adds to the unease already prevailing between the two States following A.P. taking up a tunnel project from Nagarajunasagar reservoir to draw water for Palnadu water grid with gravity and without approval of the river board and consent of Telangana.

Sources in the Telangana Irrigation department stated that the A.P. irrigation authorities had started drawing water in the guise of meeting drinking water needs. They were planning to increase the drawl to 15,000 cusecs.

As per the joint projects’ management protocol issued by the KRMB, the Nagarajunasagar project is mandated to be operated, including taking care of its maintenance works by the Telangana Irrigation department and that of Srisailam by A.P. Water Resources department. However, A.P. has been repeatedly operating the right canal unilaterally.

According the Nagarjunasagar engineers, water release to the right canal was increased to 6,395 cusecs by A.P. engineers till 6 p.m. and the Telangana engineers gradually increased water release to the left canal to 5,580 cusecs.

articles.title: SCR surpasses rooftop solar target, commissions 6.9 MW capacity
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: South Central Railway (SCR) has commissioned 6.9 MW of rooftop solar power capacity over the past 31 months, surpassing the 4.8 MW target set by the Railway Board under the Prime Minister’s rooftop solar initiative aimed at promoting renewable energy and reducing dependence on conventional power sources.

In a press release issued on Thursday, SCR General Manager Sanjay Kumar Srivastava said the zone has also taken up the installation and commissioning of an additional 2.5 MWp rooftop solar capacity, with work currently in progress.

SCR has utilised rooftop spaces across railway establishments in the Secunderabad, Hyderabad and Nanded divisions, as well as the Lalaguda Workshop, for the installation of solar power plants. These systems generate clean energy at the point of consumption while helping reduce carbon emissions and the overall environmental footprint of railway operations.

Secunderabad Division has commissioned 2.93 MWp of rooftop solar capacity, followed by Hyderabad Division with 2.60 MWp, Lalaguda Workshop with 0.87 MWp, and Nanded Division with 0.50 MWp. Railway officials said the initiative is a significant step towards Indian Railways’ goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2030.

SCR said that during the last three financial years — 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27 — its rooftop solar installations generated 7.32 million units (MU) of electricity. This helped avoid an estimated 4,963 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions, contributing to environmental sustainability and reduced energy costs.

Mr. Srivastava commended the efforts of the railway’s electrical department in implementing the solar projects and said Indian Railways has a major responsibility in developing a greener and more sustainable transportation network.

articles.title: Initiative to take Constitution Day event to taluk centres welcomed
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Constitution is not merely a book or a document but a beacon of hope for the poor, a source of confidence for the oppressed, a symbol of dignity for women and a force that shapes the future of young people, Minister for Backward Classes Welfare and Kannada and Culture and Koppal district in-charge Shivraj Tangadagi has said.

He was speaking after inaugurating the district-level Constitution Day celebrations organised by the district administration, Zilla Panchayat and the Department of Social Welfare at the cultural auditorium of the Kannada and Culture Department in Karatagi on Thursday.

Mr. Tangadagi said that the significance of Constitution Day should reach children and the general public. The values of the Constitution, the principles of democracy and the contributions of B.R. Ambedkar should always be remembered.

“Dr. Ambedkar ensured equal voting rights for every citizen, irrespective of whether they are rich or poor. The Constitution has also provided opportunities for people from ordinary families to become legislators and Ministers,” he said.

Observing that celebrations of important days have traditionally been confined to district headquarters, he welcomed the initiative to extend Constitution Day programmes to taluk centres. He said that the practice should continue and help children, young people and senior citizens understand the importance of the Constitution.
Describing the Constitution as a guiding framework for Ministers, legislators, officials and citizens, he urged everyone to understand its ideals and uphold its values.
He also called upon people to read about the history of the Constitution and remember the efforts and hardships endured by Dr. Ambedkar in drafting it.
Referring to discussions about changing the Constitution, Mr. Tangadagi warned that any attempt to alter its fundamental character will invite strong resistance and serious consequences.
Delivering a special lecture, Gavisiddappa Muttal of Yelburga taluk said that after India gained Independence in 1947, the Constitution was adopted in 1949 and subsequently, it came into force.
It guarantees fundamental rights and creates opportunities for improving people’s lives, he said.

“Equality, liberty, fraternity, educational and political rights and the right to constitutional remedies are among the important safeguards provided by the Constitution. It has also given ordinary citizens equal opportunities to attain political power and serves as the foundation for individual development and a better life,” he said.

However, even 76 years after the Constitution came into force, untouchability and social, political and economic inequalities continue to exist in several places, including rural areas, which is a matter of concern, he added.
